context: Al-Haqqah is Makkan and comes from the years when the warning was the whole message. It has no legislation in it and almost no argument in the ordinary sense. It states a thing three times in its first three verses, refusing to move on, and then spends the rest of its length showing what happened to people who were told the same thing and did not believe it.

Its final section turns from the nations to the man delivering the message. Quraysh had said he was a poet, or a soothsayer, or a man inventing revelation and attributing it to Allah. The surah answers that last charge in the strongest terms it uses anywhere, and it does so by describing what would happen to him if it were true.
name_story: Al-Haqqah, the Inevitable or the Sure Reality, from the opening word. The surah does not define it. It says al-Haqqah, then what is al-Haqqah, then what will make you know what al-Haqqah is, and the repetition is the definition: a thing whose name is stated three times before anything is said about it is a thing the listener is meant to feel the weight of before understanding it.

movements.note: Thamud and Ad, the screaming wind sent against them for seven nights and eight days, and Fir'awn and the towns overturned. The pattern is stated and then illustrated.
The trumpet blown once, the earth and the mountains lifted and crushed in a single blow, the sky splitting, and the Throne borne above them by eight.
The man given his record in his right hand who says read my record, and the man given it in his left who wishes his death had been the end of him. The two speeches are placed side by side.

movements.h: What this is, and what it is not
movements.note: The oath by what is seen and what is not seen, the denial that this is the word of a poet or a soothsayer, and the statement of what would follow if the Messenger had invented it.

themes.t: A warning that does not argue
themes.d: The surah does not reason with the listener. It describes, and the description is the argument, which is why its language is so much more physical than most of the Qur'an.
The saved man and the ruined man are each given direct speech, and the contrast is built entirely from what each of them says on arriving.
The severity of the answer is the point: if he had invented sayings and attributed them to Us, We would have seized him by the right hand and cut his lifeline.
Seven nights and eight days. A chain seventy cubits long. The specificity is doing rhetorical work: a vague warning is easy to set aside.

heart: Recited slowly, the opening three verses do something no summary conveys. The surah names a thing, asks what it is, and then asks what could make you know what it is, and the reader is held there for three lines without being given an answer. Very little writing has the confidence to delay like that.

The passage most people carry away is the man with the record in his right hand, because of what he does with it. He does not thank anyone or explain himself. He turns to the people around him and says: here, read my record. It is the sound of somebody who has stopped being afraid of being examined.

passages.why: Here, read my record. Said by a man handed the account of his own life, offering it to be read by anyone.
The Inevitable. What is the Inevitable? And what can make you know what the Inevitable is? Three lines that withhold the answer on purpose.
Had he invented sayings and attributed them to Us, We would have seized him by the right hand. The answer to the charge of forgery, and it is not a gentle one.
He did not believe in Allah the Most Great, nor did he encourage the feeding of the poor. Two failures named together, which is the surah's way of saying they are one failure.

connections.why: Al-Waqi'ah sorts humanity into three groups where this surah sorts by which hand holds the record, and the two scenes complete each other.
Al-Inshiqaq gives the same two records in shorter form and is best read immediately after this.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Haqqah. Its standing rests on its language, which is among the most concentrated in the Qur'an, and on the passage at 69:44-46, which is the Book's own answer to the charge that its Messenger composed it.
